tagline: Source of the Nile, home of gorillas
overview:
Uganda is a landlocked country on the equator in East Africa, sharing Lake Victoria, the largest lake in Africa, with Kenya and Tanzania. It is about the size of Oregon, and the White Nile begins here, flowing out of the lake at Jinja and heading north on a long journey to Egypt. Kampala, the capital, sprawls across green hills near the lakeshore.

About 48 million people live in Uganda, and the population is among the youngest in the world, with more than half under 18. English and Swahili are the official languages, Luganda is the common tongue around Kampala, and dozens of other languages are spoken across the regions. Uganda is a republic, and several traditional kingdoms, including Buganda, survive as cultural institutions. Farming employs most people, and coffee is the largest export. Winston Churchill called Uganda the pearl of Africa for its greenness, and the nickname has stuck ever since.
landAndNature: Uganda sits high on a plateau, so even on the equator the air stays mild. Lake Victoria fills the southeast, while the Rwenzori Mountains on the western border, known as the Mountains of the Moon, rise to 5,109 meters with glaciers and giant lobelia plants that tower over hikers. Volcanoes stand in the southwest, and the Great Rift Valley cradles Lakes Albert and Edward. At Murchison Falls the Nile is squeezed through a gap only about seven meters wide and explodes downward. Bwindi Impenetrable Forest shelters roughly half the world's remaining mountain gorillas, and Uganda counts over 1,000 bird species, including the towering shoebill stork.
peopleAndCulture: Matoke, steamed green bananas mashed into a soft dish, is the staple across much of the country, served with groundnut sauce, beans or chicken; the rolex, a chapati rolled around fried egg, is the favorite street snack. Most Ugandans speak three or four languages. Drumming and dance differ by region, from the fast kiganda drums of the Baganda to the Acholi bwola. Soccer fills every open field, and Ugandan runners have won Olympic gold on the track. Boda-boda motorcycle taxis weave through Kampala traffic. Families are close, and a proper greeting asks after each relative before any business begins.
history: Powerful kingdoms grew here from the 1300s, notably Buganda on the northern shore of Lake Victoria, alongside Bunyoro, Toro and Ankole. Arab and European traders arrived in the 1800s, and explorers searching for the Nile's source reached the lake in 1862. Britain made Uganda a protectorate in 1894, ruling partly through the kingdoms and bringing laborers from India to build a railway. Independence came on October 9, 1962. Idi Amin seized power in 1971 and ran a violent dictatorship for eight years, expelling the country's Asian community and killing many Ugandans, until he was overthrown in 1979. Yoweri Museveni took power in 1986, and a long insurgency troubled northern Uganda for years afterward.
funFacts: About half of the world's mountain gorillas, fewer than 1,100 in all, live in Uganda's mountain forests.
The White Nile begins its journey to the Mediterranean at Jinja, where it flows out of Lake Victoria.
Uganda has one of the youngest populations on Earth, with more than half its people under 18 years old.
At Murchison Falls the entire Nile is forced through a gap about seven meters wide before plunging 43 meters.
Uganda's national bird, the grey crowned crane, wears a spray of stiff golden feathers and appears on the flag.
